To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the high-altitude variant of hemoglobin in deer mice is associated with a higher oxygen affinity and that this variant is selectively favored at high altitudes because it confers an increased capacity for aerobic metabolism.

1) hemoglobin polymorphism is a common feature of high-altitude mammals; 2) hemoglobin variants differ in oxygen affinity, and these differences are associated with differences in physiological function; and 3) hemoglobin polymorphisms are associated with differences among individuals in fitness-related physiological performance, and these differences in physiological performance are correlated with the frequency of hemoglobin variants in the local population.

1) hemoglobin function is a key factor in mediating physiological adaptation to high altitude in mammals, 2) hemoglobin function varies among individuals of the same species, and 3) hemoglobin variation is genetically determined and can be adaptive.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
hemoglobin function in the deer mouse is a complex trait that has been molded by selection to optimize the performance of oxygen transport and delivery in the face of environmental stress.
the high-frequency hemoglobin variant in this species has evolved to provide an adaptive advantage in high-altitude environments.

the deer mouse hemoglobin polymorphism has evolved in response to selection for enhanced physiological function under hypoxic conditions, and that the biochemical basis of this adaptation is the ability of the hemoglobin polymorphism to enhance oxygen unloading in hypoxic tissues.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the evolution of high-altitude adaptation in mammals involves complex interactions among multiple genes that act in concert to modify hemoglobin function and enhance oxygen transport.

the genetic variation in the deer mouse hemoglobins that is associated with high-altitude adaptation is not due to changes in oxygen affinity per se, but rather to changes in oxygen-linked allosteric interactions that alter the kinetics of oxygen binding and release and the cooperativity of hemoglobin function.
the adaptive response to hypoxia is a dynamic process involving a complex suite of interacting genetic and phenotypic factors.
